## Hands-on 3 – The reproduction {#hands-on-3-reproduce-the-recorded-result .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 3**, in the browser lab[ or in your workspace]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.short"}: choose one of the five analysts, complete their cell on the public file `audit_original.csv`, and compare your value with the record.
:::

::: {.fs-60}
| Analyst | Emails | Test | Recorded |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|
| 8PTRZ | coded replies, Hispanic against all other names | `chisq.test()` of the 2 × 2 table | $\chi^2$ = `r fmt_num(an("8PTRZ", "statistic_recorded"), 3)` |
| UYV3F | coded replies, Hispanic against white names | logistic regression, `glm(..., family = binomial())` | *z* = `r fmt_num(an("UYV3F", "statistic_recorded"), 3)` |
| EWFMI | coded replies, three groups, Hispanic names as the base | logistic regression with the sex of the name, the poverty third and the hard-to-find address | *z* = `r fmt_num(an("EWFMI", "statistic_recorded"), 3)` |
| 25N5D | delivered emails, Hispanic against white names | `prop.test()` of two proportions | $\chi^2$ = `r fmt_num(an("25N5D", "statistic_recorded"), 3)` |
| P9W8Y | coded replies, three groups | likelihood-ratio test, `anova(..., test = "LRT")` | none |
:::

There is a cell for each of the five analysts, so choose the one whose analysis you would most like to understand: the test of a table, the logistic regression, the model with covariates, the two-proportion test on every delivered email, or the test of three groups. ## The continuity correction {#the-continuity-correction .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.small}
8PTRZ, the replies with a code:

| | Not greeted by name | Greeted by name |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Hispanic names | `r tab_8ptrz["TRUE", "0"]` | `r tab_8ptrz["TRUE", "1"]` |
| All other names | `r tab_8ptrz["FALSE", "0"]` | `r tab_8ptrz["FALSE", "1"]` |
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{.r}
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)
```

::: {.small}
With the correction, $\chi^2$ = **`r fmt_num(chi_yates, 3)`**; without it, $\chi^2$ = **`r fmt_num(chi_plain, 3)`**.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
For a two-by-two table, `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` both apply the **continuity correction** unless told otherwise: it shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by half a count before squaring. 8PTRZ and 25N5D kept the default, and so did you. For 25N5D the test gives `r fmt_num(prop_yates, 3)` with it and `r fmt_num(prop_plain, 3)` without it.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A reproduction depends on the **defaults and the codings of the software** as well as on the data and the model. The *z* of EWFMI is positive because its model takes the Hispanic names as the base group.
:::

::: notes
Here is the table of 8PTRZ: replies to Hispanic names and to all other names, greeted by name or not. The printout of chisq dot test has a first line that most people skip: Pearson's chi-square test with Yates' continuity correction. [advance] For a two-by-two table, R applies that correction by default, in chisq dot test and in prop dot test alike. It shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by half a count before squaring, which makes the test a little more cautious. Turn it off and 8PTRZ gets fourteen point nine five, 25N5D fourteen point three three. Both analysts kept the default, you kept the default, and that is why your values match the record to the third decimal. [advance] The coding matters in the same way: EWFMI took the Hispanic names as the base group, so its z is positive. A script that relies on a default is reproducible only for as long as that default stays put.
:::
